SEC17A-01.note: In 'not X but Y' the verb agrees with the affirmed Y ('sweep', singular), and the verb must be active because 'the bat's path' is its object after the interrupter. B is attractive via the plural 'ears' in the negated half; C/D require noticing the delayed object.

SEC17A-02.note: 'Every X and every Y' takes a singular verb, and the 'Since ...' clause requires present perfect. A (plural compound) is the strong lure; B and D fail on tense.

SEC17A-03.note: Subject 'such a lens' is singular and the lens is acted on, so singular passive. A is pulled by the plural 'prisms'/'frames' in the long fronted participial phrase; C/D active forms leave the lens transporting with no object.

SEC17A-04.note: The relative 'that' takes the compound 'the skull and the lower jaw' as antecedent (forced by 'their ... relative to each other'), and the narrative is past ('first exposed'), so 'were lying'. B agrees with the nearest noun 'jaw'; C is plural but present, contradicted by the bones having since been removed.

SEC17A-05.note: 'So ADJ' inversion puts the subject 'measurements' (plural) after the verb; past tense matches 'ordered' and the early readings having since been corrected. B (plural present) is the strongest lure; A/D are pulled by the singular 'hall's'.

SEC17A-06.note: The comparative 'as' clause substitutes for the action verbs 'hold back ... release', so it needs pro-verb 'do', plural for 'trumpets'. D ('as are') is attractive because inverted 'as are' is a familiar pattern and could seem to echo 'pollinated'; B/C are singular or wrong auxiliary.

SEC17A-07.note: Fronted-predicate inversion: subject is 'collapse' (singular), and 'to the present day' requires present perfect. A ('was once') has the right number but 'once' says the puzzle is over, contradicting the ongoing division; B/C are pulled by 'specialists'.

SEC17A-08.note: The transposition preceded the past 'found', so past perfect. A (present perfect) is the lure but cannot sit inside a past reported clause about a long-dead compiler; C/D are tense mismatches.

SEC17A-09.note: A long 'Although' subordinate clause ends at 'spot' and is joined to the main clause with a comma. A/B treat the dependent clause as independent; D runs 'spot a laser gauge' together and is the subtlest lure given the clause's length.

SEC17A-10.note: Two independent clauses with the contrast belonging to the second (the team succeeded despite the difficulty): semicolon before 'however', comma after. C attaches 'however' to the wrong clause; D is a comma splice; B misuses a colon for a contrast.

SEC17B-01.note: After 'the only one of the ... visitors that', the relative clause takes 'one' (singular), and the verb is active because 'pollen' is its delayed object. A (plural, agreeing with 'visitors') is the classic lure; B/C passive forms miss the object behind the interrupter.

SEC17B-02.note: In the cleft 'it is the juvenile shells ... that', the verb agrees with 'shells' (plural), and the shells are misidentified by people, so passive. A is pulled by 'it is'; D is plural but active with no object following.

SEC17B-03.note: Subject of the 'that' clause is 'photoperiod' (singular), active because 'the week' is its object after the interrupter, present perfect for 'across those decades'. B is pulled by the plural 'botanists and climatologists' of the main clause; C/D passive miss the delayed object.

SEC17B-04.note: 'More than one core' takes a singular verb, and 'Until the team switched' bounds a finished past period, so simple past. D (present perfect, singular) is the strongest lure; B is pulled by the plural meaning of 'more than one'; A is present.

SEC17B-05.note: Negative-adverbial inversion ('Not until ...') needs do-support agreeing with the long delayed subject 'eggs' (plural), present to match 'refill'. A is pulled by singular-sounding material or simply by 'does'; C is past; D 'is ... hatch' is ungrammatical once the base-form 'hatch' is found.

SEC17B-06.note: Fronted-participle inversion: subject is 'account' (singular); past, since the box 'held' the items and the account has since been transferred away. B is pulled by 'envelopes'; A and C (present / present perfect) wrongly imply it is still bundled.

SEC17B-07.note: 'Such ... that' inversion with singular subject 'pressure', and 'ever since' plus 'now survives' requires present perfect. B is pulled by 'goat herds'; C is past perfect; D is present, incompatible with 'ever since'.

SEC17B-08.note: A present-perfect announcement about a future state ('once the chamber is refilled') takes 'will'. A ('would') is the only real lure, a backshift that the present-perfect reporting verb does not license; B/D past forms clash with the future 'once' clause.
SEC17B-08.drop_reason: Only one live distractor ('would'); the two past forms die against 'once the chamber is refilled', so it plays as an easy tense item, below the module-2 hard-route bar.

SEC17B-09.note: Subject 'pigment' carries a reduced relative clause ('the illuminators ... ground by hand from imported lapis lazuli'); no punctuation may separate it from the verb 'cost'. B is the strong lure because the long modifier seems to want a closing comma, but none was opened; a colon between subject and verb (C) is never right.

SEC17B-10.note: A complete clause announcing 'one thing' is followed by the noun phrase naming it, so a colon. A is wrong because the second part is not an independent clause; B misreads it as an appositive to 'prices'; C runs it together.

tells: Agreement items with an intervening or nearby plural noun almost always key the singular (A-01 'ears', A-03 'prisms/frames', A-07 'specialists', B-01 'visitors', B-03 'botanists and climatologists', B-06 'envelopes', B-07 'herds'): 10 of 15 agreement keys are singular, so 'pick against the attracting plural noun' wins most of them. Plural keys (A-04, A-05, A-06, B-02, B-05) are the counterexamples, but in none of them does a singular noun sit as an obvious lure, so a test-taker who always rejects the option agreeing with a salient distractor noun scores very well.

Number x voice 2x2 sets (A-01, A-03, B-01, B-02, B-03): the key is active in every set where a direct object is delayed behind an interrupter (A-01, B-01, B-03) and passive where none follows (A-03, B-02). The interrupter-then-object shape is itself a cue that the active is keyed.

Time-frame cue words track the key mechanically: 'since/ever since/to the present day/across those decades' -> a 'has' form (A-02, A-07, B-03, B-07); 'until [past]'/'has since transferred' -> simple past (B-04, B-06). Legitimate, but repeated enough across the batch to be learnable as a pattern.
Punctuation items: no mark repeats as key across the four (comma A-09, semicolon+however A-10, none B-09, colon B-10), so no letter/mark tell found there.

phase2_note: All 20 keys match my cold answers; every authored explanation produces its key and correctly dispatches each distractor. One drop (B-08, too easy for the hard route). Not item-level drops but worth weighing at batch level: the template near-duplicates listed in the summary (A-01/B-01/B-03; A-05/B-07; A-06/B-05; A-07/B-06; A-02/B-04; A-03/B-02) and the singular-against-a-plural-lure pattern (10 of 15 agreement keys) make the set more learnable than any single item suggests, so avoid serving template pairs in the same form.
